examples.knowledge_point: Solving an Elementary Quadratic Inequality by Manipulating the Inequality First
examples.worked_solution:
First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6 & >3+2{x}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2} & >6+3 \\ {x}^{2} & >9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}} & >\sqrt{9} \\ |x| & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have $x>3$ or $x<-3.$

So, the solution is $x \in (-\infty,-3)\cup(3,+\infty).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from $x^2>9$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
x^2-9 > 0 .
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $y=x^2-9$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ (x+3)(x-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the roots are $x=\pm 3.$

Since the leading coefficient of $x^2-9$ is positive, the parabola opens upward. Therefore, the solution to the given inequality ($y>0$) lies outside of the roots (but does not include them).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13965374/assets/1c0d933b969094b2665e539479d5f9f715be881f9e355002c9398e0f23ba9938.png)

Therefore, the solution is $x \in (-\infty,-3)\cup(3,+\infty).$

feedback.worked_solution:
Bringing the constant term to the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-11 & \ge 0 \\ {x}^{2} & \ge 11.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \ge 11 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & \ge \sqrt{11} \\ |x| & \ge \sqrt{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have

$$
x\le -\sqrt{11}\,\text{or}\,x\ge \sqrt{11}.
$$

Therefore the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-\sqrt{11}]\cup [\sqrt{11},\infty ).$
